title: Velocity of regenerative growth varies inversely as about the square of time

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Velocity of regenerative growth varies inversely as about the square of time

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: After its early maximum, the velocity of regenerative growth (tadpole tails) falls off inversely as some power of the time since injury, approximately as 1/T^2, so that V T^2 is nearly constant.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: V^m T^n = \text{const}; for regenerating tadpole tails V T^2 \approx \text{const}

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And in this particular case, the equation _V_ _T_^2 = constant, holds very nearly true; that is to say the velocity varies, or tends to vary, inversely as the square of the time.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Regeneration”. Scope: regenerating tadpole tails, possibly regeneration generally

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: V^m T^n = \text{const}; for regenerating tadpole tails V T^2 \approx \text{const}

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch03-30: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.67

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: This is a precise quantitative law with strong discrimination among decay models. Data exist for regeneration, but the exact historical scope and sufficiently dense tadpole trajectories are not guaranteed in a single open dataset.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Derive regenerative tail length or volume velocity from time-lapse measurements after its early maximum and fit a power law V proportional to T raised to negative alpha. The claim is supported if alpha is near 2 and V times T squared is approximately constant, compared with alternative decay models.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Species, temperature, and injury extent affect the exponent.

Few public series have dense enough time sampling to estimate velocity.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.7
discriminating power: 0.9
data adequacy: 0.4
data existence: 0.45
operationalizability: 0.95

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The exponent is a clean quantitative target and distinguishes a rectangular hyperbola from neighbouring decline laws. Published tadpole-tail series, including the table Thompson analysed, contain the variables, but they have to be digitised and they do not cover regeneration at large. A small team could test the tadpole case; a general law of regenerative velocity cannot be scored from those series alone.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: After the early maximum, regress log regenerative velocity of tadpole tails on log time since amputation and test whether the slope is −2, equivalently whether velocity times time squared is constant. A slope near −2 would support the claim; a slope near −1, or an exponential decline that fits better, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Thompson offered the square law for one tadpole series and only guessed it might be general.

The first day or two after amputation is often unmeasured, which is where the maximum sits.

Length-versus-time series are in individual papers, not a shared archive.
